title: Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a surgical system that can perceive the operative field, decide what to do next, and carry out complete soft-tissue operations with outcomes matching expert surgeons, without a person continuously directing instrument motion. Its scope includes exposure, dissection, resection or repair, control of bleeding, and closure wherever those phases are required. Demonstrating the capability across more than one procedure class is part of the concept: completing a single suturing task or one phase of an operation would establish a narrower capability.

Conceptual distinction: autonomy concerns who makes and executes operative decisions, rather than the robot’s appearance or the surgeon’s location. A remotely controlled robot can perform surgery while a human still supplies the decisions and instrument commands. The July 2026 humanoid surgical demonstration illustrates this distinction: the supplied review identifies it as teleoperation. The proposed innovation could still include human supervision, approval of plans, and emergency takeover; it does not require error-free performance or the removal of all human responsibility.

significance.text: Conditional significance: expert-level whole-operation autonomy would reduce the need for an expert surgeon to continuously translate judgments into instrument movements throughout each validated operation. It would make an integrated repertoire of surgical perception, decisions, and actions reproducible through a technical system. That would be a major change in how operative expertise is delivered, even if a qualified team remained responsible for patient selection, supervision, rescue, and postoperative care.

Potential benefits require separate demonstrations. Matching expert surgeons on average safety and efficacy would not by itself show reduced variability between cases, institutions, or operators. More consistent execution is an intended benefit that would need direct measurement. Wider access outside specialist centers is a conditional downstream possibility, dependent on affordable deployment, maintenance, infrastructure, trained support teams, and timely rescue when the system encounters a problem it cannot handle.

The analogy to turning a manual craft into a reproducible technology has limits. Surgical outcomes also depend on disease, anatomy, patient physiology, treatment selection, and care before and after the operation. Autonomy over a validated repertoire would not establish competence in every operation a human surgeon can perform, nor would remote operation alone establish autonomy. The documented 2026 porcine work supports the feasibility of a surgeon-controlled robotic platform, not the broader substitution of autonomous judgment for continuous human control.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is reliable integration of all required operative phases across distinct operations, with both autonomous completion and expert-level clinical outcomes. This is a larger engineering objective than executing a bounded maneuver: the system must maintain an understanding of the patient and operative field, choose and revise a plan, recognize when a phase is complete, and manage the consequences of its actions throughout the operation. The supplied evidence does not establish whether this broader capability remains unmet worldwide as of November 1, 2026; it establishes neither its achievement nor a comprehensive search for its absence.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include tracking deforming tissue, recognizing anatomy and safe dissection planes under changing visibility, controlling force without damaging tissue, and coordinating exposure with cutting, repair, and hemostasis. Bleeding and obscured planes are useful descriptions of the target problem, but the readable evidence retained in this packet does not independently substantiate those particular assertions. They are presented here as challenges the proposed system would need to address, rather than as verified findings from the cited demonstrations.

Engineering synthesis: an integrated system also needs dependable detection of uncertainty, injury, incomplete treatment, and departures from the planned anatomy or workflow. It must recover safely when possible and request human assistance early enough when recovery exceeds its competence. The central difficulty is maintaining these abilities through interacting phases and unfamiliar variations, while defining a practical boundary beyond which autonomous operation should stop. The available teleoperation evidence does not demonstrate that autonomous decision-making and recovery capability.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes a January 26, 2022 Science Robotics study in which the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot, STAR, performed laparoscopic small-bowel anastomosis in porcine models followed over a one-week survival period. It reports that an operator selected among robot-generated plans and that phantom experiments showed greater consistency than manual laparoscopy and surgeon-operated robotic suturing. The accompanying Johns Hopkins account reportedly describes four animals and minimal human intervention. These details are retained as attributed research reports: the source index contains no captured text for either source, so the validated review could not verify the sample size, survival, comparisons, or exact intervention burden. Even if confirmed, anastomosis is a bounded component of surgery and would not establish the proposed breadth of complete operations.

The supplied research also reports that the July 9, 2025 Science Robotics paper on SRT-H, a hierarchical system using language-conditioned imitation learning, achieved 100% success across eight ex vivo porcine gallbladders without human intervention during the clipping-and-cutting phase of cholecystectomy. That percentage concerns the reported eight-specimen experiment and its defined phase, not clinical reliability or complete-operation success. The research attributes to December 1, 2025 author correspondence a clarification that the work concerned a phase of cholecystectomy in pig cadavers, with in vivo and human studies still ahead. Neither the paper nor that correspondence has captured source text in this packet, so these numerical results and qualifications could not be independently verified by the supplied review. The research identifies a journal publication and an earlier manuscript version; the missing evidence does not justify treating the result as false or as merely an unpublished preprint.

The strongest retained evidence concerns the Nature paper published July 8, 2026, which describes a humanoid laparoscopic teleoperation framework evaluated through benchtop testing, dry-laboratory user studies, and in vivo porcine studies. Its subscription preview includes a textual figure listing identifying live porcine laparoscopic cholecystectomies. A July 31 Nature Medicine research highlight states that a human surgeon controlled the robot remotely, and the associated author responses to peer review also confirm teleoperation. These materials support a dated demonstration of surgeon-controlled robotic surgery in living pigs; they do not demonstrate autonomous completion or expert-level human clinical outcomes.

Access limits constrain interpretation of the 2026 work. The retained Nature article is a subscription preview rather than an available full article body, and the research highlight is also partial. The review had a textual figure listing, not an independent inspection of the figure or operative outcomes. The peer-review correspondence has gaps in extracted text and is not the final methods section. Another supplementary PDF yielded essentially no usable text, and a purported paper download instead contained an unrelated 2020 internship report. Those files add no verified operative results and do not contradict the usable teleoperation evidence.

The packet does not establish the current status of all commercial surgical or telesurgery platforms, including the candidate’s broad statement about da Vinci and other systems. It also supplies no bounded search record supporting the assertion that no human trial of autonomous whole-operation completion had been identified by November 1, 2026. The appropriate conclusion is limited: the retained readable evidence demonstrates teleoperated porcine surgery, while the earlier autonomous milestones remain attributed reports and the present worldwide frontier cannot be determined from this packet.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: evaluate the system prospectively in living humans on two anatomically different complete operations, against expert surgeons working in the same institutions. Prespecify the full set of operative phases and require completion without continuous manual control of instrument trajectories. Define procedure-specific safety and efficacy endpoints, clinically justified non-inferiority margins, adequate sample sizes, eligibility criteria, and the permitted forms of human supervision or assistance. Thirty-day outcomes would be an initial benchmark, with longer follow-up wherever needed to assess durability of repair or treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Two anatomically different human operations autonomously completed with noninferior outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Clinical outcomes and autonomous completion should be separate endpoints. The protocol should define when a human must take over, distinguish plan approval from manual instrument control, and report every assistance event and takeover with its reason and timing. Takeovers should be counted under a prespecified autonomy-success endpoint so that successful expert rescue cannot be mistaken for autonomous completion. Patient safety can be preserved through rescue while the attempted autonomous operation still fails its completion criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Takeovers count as autonomy failures despite successful clinical rescue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: repeat the demonstration across institutions, support teams, and representative eligible patients, reporting outcomes by operation and relevant anatomical or clinical variation. State exclusions, equipment and infrastructure needs, rescue arrangements, and the circumstances in which the system declines or stops an operation. Measure variability separately if improved consistency is claimed. Success on intestinal suturing alone or one ex vivo gallbladder phase would not meet this scope; success on two complete operations would demonstrate breadth within tested conditions, not universal surgical competence.
completion_criteria.label: Complete operations reproduced across institutions with operating limits reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SUR-11, “Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field,” could provide richer information for identifying tissue and treatment boundaries. SUR-06 concerns the decisions and actions that use operative information; improved vision alone does not establish autonomous completion, and this concept does not require achievement of every capability envisioned by SUR-11.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-07, “Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body,” changes access and operative delivery, whereas SUR-06 changes who controls execution. Either could be developed without the other. SUR-10, “Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working,” changes the biological selectivity of tissue removal; autonomy might deliver that treatment, but ordinary expert-level autonomous resection would not establish cell-selective extirpation.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-01, “Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive,” addresses immune acceptance; SUR-02, “Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation,” addresses durable use of animal organs; SUR-03, “Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs,” addresses organ preservation; and SUR-12, “Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation,” addresses organ manufacture. Autonomous surgery could assist implantation or associated procedures, but cannot by itself solve tolerance, xenograft durability, cryopreservation, or organ construction.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-04, “Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection,” targets neurological recovery, and SUR-05, “Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis,” targets the biological response to injury. SUR-09, “Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply,” targets construction of replacement tissues. An autonomous system might perform interventions associated with these capabilities, but accurate operative execution does not establish neural reconnection, regenerative healing, or a viable replacement part.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-08, “Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest,” concerns creating a recoverable physiological state that permits treatment after otherwise catastrophic blood loss. SUR-06 concerns performing the treatment itself. Autonomous control of hemorrhage could become complementary, but neither metabolic arrest nor autonomous operative execution establishes the other capability.

change_log.reason: Their source texts were not captured for review. Preserving qualified detail integrates the research without treating unverified reports as established findings or false results.

change_log.reason: Phase-level success does not establish complete cholecystectomy, living-animal performance, human efficacy, or general clinical reliability.

change_log.change: Identified the July 2026 humanoid work as teleoperation and corrected the account of source access to a subscription preview with partial supporting materials.
change_log.reason: The preview, research highlight, and extracted author correspondence support human control; they do not provide complete methods or independently inspectable operative outcomes.

change_log.change: Removed categorical assertions about all commercial platforms and the absence of human autonomy trials.
change_log.reason: The packet does not verify those broad claims or document a search sufficient to establish them.

change_log.change: Made improved consistency and broader access conditional, and retained limits on universal competence and supervision.
change_log.reason: Expert-level non-inferiority does not demonstrate reduced variability, and deployment benefits depend on resources, support, and rescue capacity.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed evaluation with separate autonomy and clinical endpoints, takeover accounting, justified margins, adequate samples, reproducibility, and procedure-appropriate follow-up.
change_log.reason: Expert rescue can preserve clinical outcomes without demonstrating autonomous completion, and 30-day outcomes may not capture treatment durability.

change_log.change: Added concrete engineering barriers as labeled synthesis and distinguished SUR-06 from every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: The record needs to explain the integration challenge and relevant overlaps without presenting inferred barriers as verified study findings or merging distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: The 2022 STAR paper and Johns Hopkins report need readable source evidence to verify the four-animal account, one-week survival, phantom comparisons, plan selection, and exact human intervention burden.

The 2025 SRT-H paper and reported December correspondence need readable evidence to verify the eight-specimen success result, task boundaries, intervention accounting, and stated path toward in vivo and human work.
The worldwide status of autonomous whole-operation surgery as of November 1, 2026 remains undetermined because no bounded search record was supplied.
The status of individual commercial surgical platforms and any relevant human autonomy trials is not established by this packet.

Full methods and operative outcomes for the July 2026 humanoid study cannot be reconstructed from the preview, partial highlight, and incompletely extracted correspondence. The blank supplementary extraction provides no additional usable evidence.
The engineering discussion of bleeding, obscured planes, force control, and recovery is retained as conceptual synthesis; the supplied readable sources do not directly verify all of these barriers.
The proposed evaluation still requires selection of operations, eligibility boundaries, endpoint definitions, non-inferiority margins, sample sizes, assistance rules, and follow-up durations.

The review’s recommendation to replace the earlier autonomous milestone accounts solely with a missing-evidence statement was not adopted in full: their useful details are retained with explicit attribution and verification limits, as required to preserve uncertain research without overstating it.

brief.title: Robots that carry out whole operations at expert level
possible: Patients could undergo a complete operation in which a robot decides and carries out each surgical step, with results matching expert surgeons. It would handle everything required, from exposing the tissue to controlling bleeding and closing the wound. A surgical team could supervise and take over when needed.
why: Expert surgeons would no longer need to direct every instrument movement throughout an operation. A system could reproduce their combined skills in recognising tissue, choosing actions and carrying them out, changing how surgical expertise reaches patients.

sources.who: The Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot research team
sources.showed: This is a study of autonomous robotic joining of small-bowel ends in pigs.
sources.cited_for: It supports the feasibility of automating a defined surgical task.
sources.not_established: Joining bowel ends does not establish autonomous completion of whole operations.

sources.showed: This is a report on the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot performing intestinal surgery in pigs.
sources.cited_for: It describes animal experiments with limited human intervention.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish expert-level outcomes across different complete human operations.

sources.showed: This is a study of autonomous clipping and cutting during a phase of gallbladder removal in pig cadavers.
sources.cited_for: It supports autonomous completion of a defined phase of surgery.
sources.not_established: A phase performed in cadavers does not establish whole-operation performance in living patients.

sources.who: Zekai Liang, Michael Yip and collaborators
sources.showed: They built a remotely controlled surgical system using a human-shaped robot and tested it in laboratory tasks and surgery in living pigs.
sources.cited_for: It supports the feasibility of surgeon-controlled surgery using a human-shaped robot.
sources.not_established: The surgeon supplied the decisions and instrument commands, so the work does not establish autonomous surgery.

sources.who: Zekai Liang, Michael Yip and collaborators
sources.showed: A research highlight reports that a surgeon remotely controlled a human-shaped robot during gallbladder removal in pigs.
sources.quote: A humanoid robot, controlled remotely by a human surgeon, performed laparoscopic gallbladder removal in pigs — which revealed key insights for future optimization and clinical translation.
sources.cited_for: It confirms that the animal operations used human control.
sources.not_established: Successful remote control does not establish independent surgical decisions or expert-level human outcomes.

shown: The Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot team reported joining small-bowel ends in living pigs, with an operator selecting among robot-generated plans. The SRT-H team reported completing the clipping-and-cutting phase of gallbladder removal without intervention in eight pig cadaver specimens. Both demonstrations covered parts of operations.

Zekai Liang, Michael Yip and collaborators demonstrated gallbladder removal in living pigs using a human-shaped robot. A surgeon controlled it remotely. This showed a different capability from a robot choosing and executing the operation itself.
missing: A system still needs to demonstrate all required phases of different complete operations with outcomes matching expert surgeons.
It must demonstrate that it can recognise problems, recover safely and request help before exceeding its abilities.
Trials must distinguish independent completion from successful surgery achieved through human rescue.
Performance must hold across hospitals, support teams and eligible patients, with clear limits on when the system can operate.

milestones.label: Expert-level results across two different complete human operations
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to show complete operations in different anatomical areas, without continuous human instrument control, matching local experts on safety and effectiveness. This would establish breadth beyond a surgical task.

milestones.label: Human takeovers counted as failures of autonomous completion
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to report every assistance event and count manual takeovers as failures of autonomous completion. This would keep successful human rescue from being mistaken for independent performance.

milestones.label: Complete operations repeated across hospitals with clear operating limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to repeat across hospitals, teams and eligible patients, with exclusions, rescue arrangements and stopping rules reported. This would establish where the capability works reliably.

uncertain: The operations, eligible patients and acceptable differences from expert outcomes still need to be defined.
Matching expert outcomes would not establish whether autonomous surgery also makes results more consistent.
It remains unclear how reliably a system could handle changing anatomy, bleeding and unexpected problems throughout an operation.

page.title: Autonomous soft-tissue surgery
page.definition: A robot chooses a plan for the individual patient, selects and executes every operative phase, and monitors tissue that changes shape as it is handled. Across different types of soft-tissue operation, clinical safety and efficacy must fall within prespecified noninferiority margins relative to expert surgery. A surgeon may approve the plan, supervise and take over in an emergency. In a reported rabbit appendectomy, the robot controlled the instruments while a surgeon chose each phase.

goal.need: A 2025 estimate put the global shortfall across all surgery at 160 million or more operations a year. Teleoperated instruments still occupy a surgeon throughout an operation. If a local general surgeon could supervise kidney tumour removal, rural patients could avoid travel to a specialist centre. In a mass casualty emergency, patients with survivable injuries could receive care sooner when surgeons are scarce. Both uses depend on a team and hospital equipped to manage complications.

completion.title: A robot completes whole soft-tissue operations with clinical outcomes noninferior to expert surgery.
completion.criterion: For each operation in a repertoire covering different procedure types, a registered comparative clinical study meets its prespecified noninferiority criteria for safety and efficacy against expert surgeons. The robot selects and executes every required operative phase after initial plan approval. Human operative control constitutes failure of autonomous completion, even if rescue succeeds clinically. Eligibility, endpoints, clinically justified margins, sample sizes and follow-up are specified in procedure-specific protocols.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; combined application of the LASR Level 4 autonomy definition and IDEAL Stage 3 comparative evaluation.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA robotics documents, autonomy classifications, IDEAL, DARPA Surgical Competition material, ARPA-H ALISS and trial registries found no joint threshold for whole-operation autonomy, expert clinical outcomes and repertoire breadth. LASR Level 4 supplies the autonomy definition; IDEAL Stage 3 supplies comparative evaluation. Neither specifies the required repertoire size or universal clinical margins.

milestones.title: A robot performs a soft-tissue surgical task without continuous human instrument control.
milestones.criterion: A human initiates a defined soft-tissue surgical task. The robot executes the task without requiring the operator to continuously direct instrument movements or activations.
milestones.set_by: Lee and colleagues, LASR taxonomy, Level 2 task autonomy or higher; a research classification rather than an FDA performance standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: without requiring the surgeon’s continuous direct control over the movements and instrument activations.

milestones.title: Preclinical testing demonstrates the safety and feasibility of a complete autonomous operation.
milestones.criterion: Evaluate the autonomous software and robot hardware separately, then together on realistic tasks in simulation. For the complete operation, demonstrate that the integrated robot selects and executes the required phases. Assess safety against the likelihood and severity of identified failures, including the reliability of transfer to human control.
milestones.set_by: IDEAL Robotics Colloquium, 2024 consensus statement, preclinical evaluation at Stage 0; applied here to whole-operation autonomy.
milestones.threshold_quote: preclinical evaluation (IDEAL stage 0) to assess safety and feasibility

milestones.title: A robot completes a whole soft-tissue operation in a person as a proof of concept.
milestones.criterion: First-in-human use of the integrated robot achieves technical proof of concept for the complete operation, with apparent safety, potential efficacy and patient outcomes assessed. IDEAL Stage 1 encompasses a single case or a few cases.
milestones.set_by: IDEAL Collaboration, 2019 framework, Stage 1 endpoint; a general surgical-innovation criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: technical achievement, apparent safety and potential efficacy.

milestones.title: Clinical development produces a whole-operation robot and technique ready for replication.
milestones.criterion: Prospective clinical development yields a procedure and indications stable enough for replication by other teams. Intentional iterative modification is complete, although limited subsequent modifications remain permissible.
milestones.set_by: IDEAL Collaboration, 2019 framework, Stage 2a endpoint; a general surgical-innovation criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: stable enough to permit multi-centre replication

milestones.title: Multicentre use establishes that whole-operation autonomy can proceed to comparative evaluation.
milestones.criterion: Multicentre prospective evaluation establishes wider adoption of the stable procedure and feasibility of a definitive comparative trial. The Stage 2b endpoint includes assessed learning curves, agreed intervention and quality standards, a target population, comparator, primary endpoint and willingness to accept randomisation.
milestones.set_by: IDEAL Collaboration, 2019 framework, Stage 2b endpoints; a general surgical-innovation criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: progression to a formal randomised controlled trial is feasible

milestones.title: A robot judges when one soft-tissue surgical task is complete and initiates the next.
milestones.criterion: During a sequence of surgical tasks, the robot assesses whether the current task is complete, chooses the next task and begins it without a human specifying the transition.
milestones.set_by: Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, ALISS award to Vanderbilt University
milestones.threshold_quote: allows the robot to progress from one task to another.

not_found: Web-indexed searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and ISRCTN did not identify a registered comparative study establishing autonomous whole-operation completion with expert-level clinical outcomes across the listed organs.
The Science publisher pages for STAR and SRT-H could not be opened; author manuscripts were accessible.
The full methods of the humanoid surgery paper remained behind subscription access; its accessible abstract explicitly identifies teleoperation.

results.finding: The supervised dual-arm robot executed 77 electrosurgical cuts across eight kidney phantom resections.
results.detail: The verdict applies to individual cuts. Supervisor approval and manual energy enablement were required.
results.quote:
eight consecutive autonomous tumor resections comprising 77
electrosurgical cuts; all cuts succeeded, achieving NSMs in
all eight procedures (100 % success rate).

results.finding: The robot sequenced resection tasks in eight kidney phantom runs with 20 supervisor-requested replans.
results.detail: The state machine advanced to imaging and replanning after a completed cut. The next cut remained gated by supervisor approval.
results.quote:
Supervisor re-plan requests: 20
total (average 2.50 per procedure) and 0, respectively.

results.finding: The integrated Multi-shot robot achieved negative margins in 8/8 hydrogel kidney phantom tumor resections.
results.detail: The phantoms did not bleed. The workflow omitted access, vascular control, kidney repair and closure. A supervisor stopped one baseline run, and three Multi-shot grasp failures required manual re-engagement.
results.quote:
Multi-shot (Main Method): In eight experiments, all tumor
resections resulted in NSMs, and average margin size was
6.63 ± 1.88 mm.

results.finding: The robot executed surgeon-selected appendectomy tasks through the energized cut in 3 of 4 live rabbits.
results.detail: In the fourth rabbit, the joint-limit governor aborted at handover before the policy could act, and the surgeon completed the operation by hand.
results.quote: With the surgeon selecting the surgical phase, the policy completed the appendectomy in three of the four animals.

results.finding: The video-based phase predictor agreed with surgeon phase labels on 24.6% of policy control steps during deployment in four live rabbits.
results.detail: The policy used a fixed phase order. Under the deployment endoscope, the surgeon supplied the phase by keypress while the predictor continued to supply timing estimates.
results.quote: First, the surgeon supplied the phase in vivo, because the vision-based phase predictor agreed with the surgeon on only 24.6% of policy control steps under the deployment endoscope, a domain shift known from phase recognition across hospitals

results.finding: The integrated robot completed appendectomy under shared autonomy in 3 of 4 live rabbits.
results.detail: The simulator scored progress through approach and jaw closure without a trocar violation. In the fourth live deployment, the joint-limit governor stopped the arm at handover before any policy command reached tissue.
results.quote: Third, retrained on 849 in-vivo demonstrations, the configuration completed the appendectomy in three of four live rabbits under shared autonomy, with the cutting jaw closed at every cautery sample and a peak RCM error of 0.84 mm.

results.finding: The robot completed automated small-bowel laser soldering in 5 of 6 enrolled pigs.
results.detail: One pig died of heart failure during anesthesia. The authors attributed the death to an event unrelated to the experimental procedure.
results.quote: The five pigs that successfully completed the procedure, survived without leaks and histology indicated mucosal regeneration and fibrous tissue adhesion.

results.finding: In the six-pig Heineke-Mikulicz study, 0 of the five pigs that completed robotic soldering developed leaks.
results.detail: The study used open exposure and manual preparation. The robot executed a preset soldering path. The authors described a stop button but reported no test of transfer to human control.
results.quote: The five pigs that successfully completed the procedure, survived without leaks and histology indicated mucosal regeneration and fibrous tissue adhesion.

results.finding: Toumai with MicroGenius autonomously clipped and transected the bile duct in one pig, with 88% individual-step success.

In this experiment, the system 
precisely performed the full-process autonomous procedure of bile duct clipping and transection

results.finding: Toumai with MicroGenius completed the bile duct clipping and transection sequence in one pig on its first attempt.

autonomous dynamic adjustments and corrections, leading to the successful completion of the

results.finding: Toumai with MicroGenius completed the bile duct clipping and transection task in one laboratory pig on its first attempt.
results.detail: The filing reports an aggregate step success rate. It leaves the number of steps and the nature and severity of unsuccessful steps unspecified.
results.quote:
The success rate for individual operational steps reached 88%, with real-time 
autonomous dynamic adjustments and corrections, leading to the successful completion of the 
overall surgery in a single attempt

results.finding: In 15 ex vivo porcine gallbladder trials, the robot used a 0.5 mm boundary deviation threshold to transition from pulling to dissection.
results.detail: The paper gives dissection metrics for 15 trials. It does not report a separate transition success rate. The partial verdict concerns next-task selection.
results.quote: Once the grasping and pulling are accomplished, the FBF remains static. Similar to grasping, we first align the PCH to the gallbladder’s surface before performing the dissection.

results.finding: Robot-executed gallbladder retraction achieved 92% success across 52 attempts on ex vivo porcine livers.
results.detail: The medical expert rated success by retraction direction and force. The ex vivo robot controller used a 2.5 N force limit in an open setup with laparoscopic instruments.
results.quote:
In total,
48 out of the 52 gallbladder retraction trajectories during
the ex vivo porcine liver surgeries were rated as successful
by the medical expert, resulting in a success rate of 92%.

results.finding: The da Vinci Research Kit autonomously aligned both tissue targets on one ex vivo lamb kidney in 47 seconds in a representative trial.
results.detail: The trial used a fixed camera and planar instrument motion. The paper gives the representative trial time but does not specify the total number of kidney trials.
results.quote: For this experiment, the target points overlayed on the insertion points in 47 s with identical computation time to previous experiments.

results.finding: Robot-executed electrocautery cleared airway obstruction in 5 of 5 ex vivo porcine trachea models.
results.detail: The evidence covers supervised electrocautery in an open setup. The operator manually tensioned the pseudotumor between cuts. The supplied arXiv version identifies itself as a preprint accepted for journal publication.
results.quote: By qualitatively comparing the side views provided, it is evident that the tumor was successfully removed from the trachea in all five consecutive trials.

results.finding: Probot transurethral prostate electrovaporization in five patients averaged 1.7 g/min.
results.detail: The prose labels 1.7 g/min as a time, but the units indicate a tissue removal rate. The supplied journal supplement abstract does not establish its peer-review status.
results.quote:
The mean
vaporization time (1.7 g/min). the irrigation time (147 min). the dura-
tion of post-operative catheterization (1 1 h) and a mean hospital stay
of 2 days were encouraging.

definition = "A robot chooses a plan for the individual patient, selects and executes every operative phase, and monitors tissue that changes shape as it is handled. Across different types of soft-tissue operation, clinical safety and efficacy must fall within prespecified noninferiority margins relative to expert surgery. A surgeon may approve the plan, supervise and take over in an emergency. In a reported rabbit appendectomy, the robot controlled the instruments while a surgeon chose each phase.". Reason: The definition leaves unclear who chooses the initial plan and how whole-operation autonomy differs from a robot executing surgeon-selected phases.

goal.need = "A 2025 estimate put the global shortfall across all surgery at 160 million or more operations a year. Teleoperated instruments still occupy a surgeon throughout an operation. If a local general surgeon could supervise kidney tumour removal, rural patients could avoid travel to a specialist centre. In a mass casualty emergency, patients with survivable injuries could receive care sooner when surgeons are scarce. Both uses depend on a team and hospital equipped to manage complications.". Reason: The 2025 estimate updates the scale of unmet need, and the rural kidney and emergency trauma examples explain which patients might benefit and under what conditions.

add statement by Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, SARRTS award to Children’s National Research Institute, 2024: "demonstrate a supervised autonomous kidney resection". Reason: The SARRTS award supplies a specific government goal for the kidney case and identifies the conditions of its planned demonstration.

add statement by Artificial Intelligence Surgery editorial-board expert panel, white paper on autonomous actions in clinical surgery, 2022: "surgery should not be done without the control of a human surgeon". Reason: The existing statements omit a published panel position on the surgeon’s responsibility during autonomous surgery.
add case "Trachea". Reason: The ALISS team explicitly targets autonomous removal of tracheal tumours in simulation.
add case "Prostate". Reason: The ALISS team explicitly targets autonomous removal of prostate tumours in simulation, and prostate resection also has an early laboratory demonstration.

edit m1: criterion = "A human initiates a defined soft-tissue surgical task. The robot executes the task without requiring the operator to continuously direct instrument movements or activations.". Reason: The criterion mixes the task-autonomy test with individual experiments and their publication status.

add milestone after m1: "A robot judges when one soft-tissue surgical task is complete and initiates the next.". Reason: The sequence jumps from one human-initiated task to a whole operation and misses the separately testable decision to move from one task to the next.

edit m2: title = "Preclinical testing demonstrates the safety and feasibility of a complete autonomous operation."; criterion = "Evaluate the autonomous software and robot hardware separately, then together on realistic tasks in simulation. For the complete operation, demonstrate that the integrated robot selects and executes the required phases. Assess safety against the likelihood and severity of identified failures, including the reliability of transfer to human control."; threshold_quote = "preclinical evaluation (IDEAL stage 0) to assess safety and feasibility"; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: IDEAL assigns safety and feasibility to preclinical evaluation, while the existing criterion also requires it to establish acceptability and includes individual study results.
